paper: Adil & Hussein (2020), Numerical Solution for Two-Sided Stefan Problem, Iraqi J. Science 61(2):444-452, DOI 10.24996/ijs.2020.61.2.24

open_questions.q: How does the Landau-transform + Crank-Nicolson scheme perform when the two moving boundaries h1(t), h2(t) are NOT prescribed a priori but are instead coupled to the temperature field through a genuine Stefan condition (i.e. h_i'(t) proportional to a jump in u_x across the interface, with a latent-heat parameter)?
open_questions.basis: Section 1 (What the paper does) and Genuine Critique P3 in REPORT.md/REPORT.tex: in both of the paper's test cases the free boundaries h1=1+t, h2=2+2t (Ex 1) and h1=1+t^3, h2=2+t^2 (Ex 2) are PRESCRIBED, so the numerical problem actually solved is a variable-coefficient parabolic PDE on a moving domain, not a true free-boundary problem. The paper's title 'two-sided Stefan problem' would only be fully honored by a coupled formulation. This is genuinely open in the paper's numerical evidence.
next_steps: Extend work/stefan_cn.py to include a discrete Stefan condition at each moving boundary: (h1', h2') computed each step from a finite-difference approximation of the transformed v_y at y=0 and y=1, divided by h3(t).
Verify against a known analytic two-phase Stefan solution (e.g. Neumann's solution for a semi-infinite slab with constant thermal properties) rather than a manufactured u.
Report how the observed convergence order and stability change when the boundary motion becomes an implicit unknown.

open_questions.q: How does the scheme handle the well-known moving-boundary singularity at t=0+, where the interface velocity diverges like 1/sqrt(t) for classical Stefan problems? The paper's manufactured solutions are smooth at t=0 and therefore hide this issue.
open_questions.basis: Genuine Critique P2 in REPORT.md/REPORT.tex explicitly notes that the two test cases are pure MMS with low-order polynomial-in-x exact solutions, both smooth at t=0. Classical two-phase Stefan problems with piecewise-constant initial data (e.g. a warm liquid abutting a cold solid at the melting temperature) have h_i'(t) ~ 1/sqrt(t) near t=0. The paper says nothing about this regime, so the behavior of the Landau map (which divides by h3(t)) and of the second-order-in-time CN discretization on non-smooth initial data is untested.
next_steps: Run the solver with a Neumann-like initial condition that produces a 1/sqrt(t) boundary velocity and measure error near t=0 with graded time steps tau_n = tau_0 * n^alpha.
Compare uniform-tau CN vs. a variable-step BDF2 or a time-adaptive CN on the same problem to quantify how much of the second-order rate survives near the singularity.
Report whether an initial-time boundary layer requires spatial mesh grading in y as well.

open_questions.q: Does the Landau-transform + CN methodology extend to 2D and 3D moving domains with anisotropic thermal conductivity, and if so, what is the practical cost compared to level-set or phase-field alternatives?
open_questions.basis: Genuine Critique P5 in REPORT.md/REPORT.tex: the scheme and analysis are strictly 1D. The Landau map in 1D reduces to a single scalar y = (x-h1)/h3; in 2D or 3D on a domain whose boundary evolves in a non-affine way there is no equally clean fixed-domain map, and even when one exists (e.g. body-fitted mapping of a shrinking disk or a smooth solidification front) the transformed PDE picks up mixed spatial derivatives and time-dependent metric terms. The paper does not address any of this.
next_steps: Formulate the Landau transform for a 2D two-phase problem with a smooth radial front r=R(t) and derive the analog of the paper's eq. (4), tracking all metric-induced first-derivative terms.
Implement a 2D CN discretization on the fixed reference domain and benchmark against a level-set or front-tracking reference on an anisotropic (tensor-diffusion) Stefan problem.

Report wall-time and memory scaling vs. mesh, and compare with published level-set two-phase Stefan solvers to quantify whether the Landau approach remains competitive when the moving boundary is no longer a graph.

open_questions.q: Front-tracking vs. level-set formulations: the paper implicitly assumes the free boundary is a single-valued graph x=h_i(t) with h1<h2 for all t. How does the method behave if the interface topology changes (merger, pinch-off, non-graph geometry)?
open_questions.basis: Section 1 (Landau change of variables) requires h3(t)=h2(t)-h1(t) > 0 for all t, so the transform is singular the moment h1 and h2 collide or the interface stops being a graph. This is a structural limitation of the front-tracking-in-Landau-coordinates formulation and is not discussed in the paper. Level-set formulations, in contrast, handle topology change natively.
next_steps: Construct a manufactured or physical scenario in which h3(t) -> 0 at some t = t* < T and run the paper's method to observe the failure mode (blow-up in transformed coefficients like a/h3^2 and b/h3).
Implement a level-set variant on the same benchmark and compare accuracy, robustness, and cost.
Report a boundary in parameter space (Stefan number, initial gap h3(0), forcing) that separates 'front-tracking is fine' from 'level-set is required'.

open_questions.q: How does the scheme perform when the two-phase Stefan model is coupled with convection in the liquid phase (i.e. u_t = a u_xx + b(x,t; u) u_x + c u + f with b including a natural-convection or forced-convection velocity), rather than treating b as a purely geometric coefficient?
open_questions.basis: Section 1 shows the paper allows a nonzero b(x,t) u_x term but treats it as a KNOWN function, not as a solution-dependent transport term. Physically, most real two-phase Stefan problems (solidification of a melt, ice-water systems with buoyancy, alloy freezing with solute rejection) have b coupled to the temperature or solute field. The Crank-Nicolson tridiagonal solve in the paper is linear and does not address this nonlinearity, and neither of the manufactured examples exercises it.
next_steps: Extend work/stefan_cn.py to allow b to be a functional b(x,t,u) and solve the resulting nonlinear tridiagonal system per step via Picard or Newton iteration.
Benchmark against a reference Stefan-Boussinesq problem (e.g. melting of a pure substance with buoyant flow) using a published high-fidelity solution.
Report the range of Peclet numbers over which CN remains stable and second-order without upwinding, and identify when a semi-Lagrangian or SUPG-stabilized variant becomes necessary.
